options.text: If a parent has ADHD, there is 50% chance that the child will develop ADHD.

questions.explanation: The heritability is 75%.

questions.question_text: Which of the following randomization methods is the least likely to produce bias in a randomized control trial (RCT)?

options.text: Allocation of patients by their month of birth
Allocation of patients by hospitalization status (inpatient versus outpatient)
Allocation of patients by gender (subdivided into strata and individuals within each striatum undergo further randomization)
Allocation of patients by laboratory results (e.g. blood cholesterol status)
Allocation of patients by order of arrival time in clinic

correct_answer.text: Allocation of patients by gender (subdivided into strata and individuals within each striatum undergo further randomization)

correct_answers.text: Allocation of patients by gender (subdivided into strata and individuals within each striatum undergo further randomization)

questions.explanation: Stratified randomization, while the other options are quasi-randomization. For stratified randomization, subjects are subdivided into strata, and individuals within each striatum are then randomized. This is less likely to produce bias in RCT compared with quasi-randomization, which is not a proper randomization method as it is based on subjects’ characteristics, such as month of birth, hospitalization status and laboratory results.

questions.question_text: Which of the following does not increase the power of a randomized controlled trial?

options.text: Comparison of active treatment with placebo
An increase in the number of collaborating centres instead of the number of subjects
Using observer rated questionnaires instead of self-reported questionnaires

correct_answer.text: An increase in the number of collaborating centres instead of the number of subjects

correct_answers.text: An increase in the number of collaborating centres instead of the number of subjects

questions.explanation: The power of an RCT depends on sample size, total number of endpoints, difference in compliance between two groups, increased number of endpoints by selecting a high-risk population or increased duration of follow-up. Having more collaborating centres does not necessarily mean more subjects, which is important in increasing the power of an RCT.

questions.question_text: Based on your understanding of the clinical antipsychotic trials of intervention effectiveness (CATIE) trial, which of the following antipsychotics has been shown to be associated with the lowest rate of discontinuation?
questions.explanation: Based on the findings of the trial, which compared second-generation antipsychotics with first-generation antipsychotics, olanzapine has been shown to be the most effective in terms of the rate of discontinuation.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a feature associated with Parkinson disease?

options.text: Depression has a unimodal age of onset
Resting and pill-rolling tremor of 4–6 Hz

correct_answer.text: Depression has a unimodal age of onset

correct_answers.text: Depression has a unimodal age of onset

questions.explanation: Depression in Parkinson disease has bimodal onset. Patients may become depressed at the time of diagnosis, although it may occur late in the course and be associated with severe bradykinesia and gait disturbances. Depressive symptoms precede motor symptoms in 30% of cases. The prevalence of major depressive disorder in Parkinson disease is 20%, with prevalence increased to 40% if dysthymia and minor depression are included. Comorbidity with anxiety occurs in two-thirds of cases. SSRIs are the first-line treatment for depression in this group of patients. Tricyclic antidepressants should be avoided as they may cause confusion and cognitive impairment.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a feature of Steele–Richardson–Olszewski syndrome?
questions.explanation: Steele–Richardson–Olszewski syndrome is also known as progressive supranuclear palsy (PSP). It is associated with parkinsonism without prominent tremor, vertical gaze palsy, midline more than appendicular rigidity, early postural instability, frequent falls, poor eye contact and monotonous speech. Unlike in Parkinson disease, there is little or no response to levodopa.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Huntington disease is false?

options.text: Electroencephalogram (EEG) shows absence of rhythmic background activity along with low-voltage intermittent random activities.
Genetic counselling for family members should be offered.
It is not commonly associated with psychiatric comorbidity.
Tetrabenazine helps to reduce the movement disorder.
There is marked atrophy of head of caudate nucleus and putamen.

correct_answer.text: It is not commonly associated with psychiatric comorbidity.

correct_answers.text: It is not commonly associated with psychiatric comorbidity.

questions.explanation: Psychiatric disturbance is variable but common. Initial insight may result in depression. There may also be prodromal personality changes, antisocial behaviour with substance misuse and affective and schizoaffective disorders. Mild euphoria with explosive outbursts, irritability and rage may also be noted. In addition, there is a slowly progressive intellectual impairment.

questions.question_text: A 31-year-old woman is charged in court for homicide. She pleads that, at the time of the offence, she had epilepsy. Which of the following statements about this phenomenon is false?

options.text: Her plea is known as sane automatism.
The automatism plea is generally restricted to homicide cases.
The mind was not conscious of what the body is doing.
There are two types of automatism pleas.

correct_answer.text: Her plea is known as sane automatism.

correct_answers.text: Her plea is known as sane automatism.

questions.explanation: Automatism is a plea generally restricted to cases of homicide. The defendant pleads that, at the time of the offence, their behaviour was automatic. The law uses this term to mean a state almost near-unconsciousness. It refers to unconscious, involuntary, non-purposeful acts where the mind is not conscious of what the body is doing. The case law now differentiates sane automatism caused by external factors (extrinsic factors), such as hypoglycaemia owing to insulin use, from insane automatism caused by disease of the mind resulting from illness or brain disease (intrinsic factors), such as diabetes mellitus, epilepsy and even hysterical dissociative fugue states. This case is an example of insane automatism plea.

questions.question_text: What is the increase in likelihood of a male with learning disability committing an offence compared with a male with no disorder?
questions.explanation: Men with learning disabilities are three times more likely to offend than men with no disorder or handicap and five times more likely to commit a violent offense. Women with learning disabilities are almost four times more likely to offend than women with no disorder or handicap and 25 times more likely to commit a violent offense. As they lack an understanding of the nature of their behaviour and its legal consequences, they are more suggestible and are easier to catch. Learning disabilities may also lead to violence and even homicide. In addition, in panic and frustration, such people may commit arson or sexual offences that relate to their difficulty initiating and sustaining interpersonal and sexual relationships.

questions.question_text: Which of the following can be used to assess psychopathy in a non-forensic population?
questions.explanation: The PCL-R was devised by Hare and is used to measure the presence and level of psychopathy in forensic populations. A short version, the PCL-SV, can be used in non-forensic populations. The HCR-20 and VRAG measure violence risk, whereas the STATIC-99 is used to assess sexual recidivism.

questions.question_text: An infarct in which of the following regions of the brain is most likely to result in depression?
questions.explanation: Patients with depression have been reported as having a higher number and larger volume of infarcts affecting the prefrontosubcortical circuits, particularly the caudate and pallidum in basal ganglia and genu of internal capsule, with left-sided predominance.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false regarding the relationship between psychiatric disorders and criminal behaviour?

options.text: Antisocial behaviour may appear before any sign of psychiatric or neurological disturbance in Huntington disease.
Offending is more likely in mild and moderate learning disability than in severe learning disability.
Prisoners with epilepsy have committed more violent crimes than those without epilepsy.
Patients with schizophrenia have similar rates of offending to the general population.
Patients with schizophrenia are six times more likely to be charged for violence.

correct_answer.text: Prisoners with epilepsy have committed more violent crimes than those without epilepsy.

correct_answers.text: Prisoners with epilepsy have committed more violent crimes than those without epilepsy.

questions.explanation: There is no excess of violent crimes in prisoners with epilepsy. The increase in prevalence of epilepsy in prisoners (two times that of general population) is due to common social and biological adversity, leading to both epilepsy and crime.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false regarding the conduction of an RCT?

options.text: A multi-centred trial is preferred to assess effects of trial drug in different ethnic groups because of variation in pharmacokinetics.
A patient can withdraw from the RCT at any time, and a valid reason is required.
Placebo treatment is not recommended in chronic and severe illnesses.
The RCT needs to obtain ethic committee approval beforehand.
The RCT should be guided by the uncertainty principle, and both investigators and subjects should not know the efficacy of trial drug and gold-standard treatment.

correct_answer.text: A patient can withdraw from the RCT at any time, and a valid reason is required.

correct_answers.text: A patient can withdraw from the RCT at any time, and a valid reason is required.

questions.explanation: This option is contrary to the Declaration of Helsinki, which states that research subjects can withdraw from study without giving any reason. Steps involved in the conduction of RCT include identify and engage investigational sites, develop trial governance procedures, develop trial procedures according to good clinical practice, apply and obtain funding, develop recruitment strategies and methods to identify and overcome recruitment problems, develop data capture methods, engage in oversight of trial progress, develop procedures for adverse event reporting and complete trial termination procedures.

questions.question_text: For depression, relapse refers to the return of depressive symptoms. The risk has been estimated to be particularly high within how many months following the initial withdrawal of antidepressants?
questions.explanation: Risk of relapse is particularly high, with rates between 40% and 60% following the withdrawal of antidepressants within the first 4 months of achieving an initial response. The risk is much reduced if antidepressant therapy is continued, to around 10%–30%.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman has been diagnosed with depression, and she has been researching more about depression online. She finds out about a previous trial, called STAR*D, which was conducted. She wants to know more about the trial. Which of the following statements about the trial is incorrect?

options.text: A third of the patients managed to reach a remission or virtual absence of the symptoms during the initial phase of the study.
One in three depressed patients who previously did not achieve remission using an antidepressant became symptom free with the help of augmenting with another antidepressant.
One in four depressed patients became symptom free after 9 weeks.
The level 4 findings suggested that either venlafaxine or mirtazapine treatment may be a better choice than a monoamine oxidase inhibitor (MAOI).

questions.explanation: A third of the participants reached a remission or virtual absence of their symptoms during the initial phase of the study, with an additional 10%–15% experiencing some improvement. The remission rate was noted to be 30% higher than expected, and this might be due to the systematic and comprehensive approach to care.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the pharmacological treatment of delirium is incorrect?

options.text: Benzodiazepines should be avoided because they can exacerbate delirium.
Behaviour, not amenable to other interventions such as gentle reassurance, may respond to treatment like antipsychotics.
Haloperidol is the most frequently used in this situation, as it is generally effective and safe.
Second-generation antipsychotics are indicated for patients who are prone to extrapyramidal side effects.
Psychotropic medications should be commenced for the treatment of hypoactive delirium.

correct_answer.text: Psychotropic medications should be commenced for the treatment of hypoactive delirium.

correct_answers.text: Psychotropic medications should be commenced for the treatment of hypoactive delirium.

questions.explanation: Hypoactive delirium is characterized by apathy, confusion and lethargy. Hypoactive delirium is often mistaken for depression. Treatment of hypoactive delirium with psychotropic medications is not recommended. In addition, general principles of prescription in delirium include mono-therapy, prescription with lowest dose and tapering off the medications when delirium resolves.

questions.question_text: Approximately what percentage of elderly patients suffer from somatization disorders?
questions.explanation: The most common somatic complaints in the elderly include pain, constipation, fatigue, headache, impaired balance, dry mouth, nausea, fatigue, headache, impaired balance, dry mouth, change in appetite and difficulty in urinating. Somatic complaints may be a presentation of underlying depressive (masked depression) and anxiety disorders.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding the work of Hayflick is true?

options.text: Cells double at a rate that is inversely proportional to age.
Cells double at a rate that is proportional to age.
Cells triple at a rate that is proportional to age.
Death of a cell line is not usually caused by faulty laboratory techniques.
No human cell may be immortal.

correct_answer.text: Cells double at a rate that is inversely proportional to age.

correct_answers.text: Cells double at a rate that is inversely proportional to age.

questions.explanation: Several studies have replicated Hayflick’s work, which showed that the number of population doublings of cultured human cells is inversely proportional to the person’s age. The death of a cell line is usually caused by faulty laboratory techniques. The only human cells that may be immortal are the transformed or abnormal mixoploid cells, such as the HeLa cells. This cell line was derived from cervical cancer cells taken in 1951 from Henrietta Lacks, a patient who eventually died of her cancer.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman was scolded by her boss for being slow and for making mistakes at work. Her boss threatens to dismiss her. At home that night, she tells her husband all the details involving her boss scolding her and her thinking about what she could have done. Which of the following defence mechanisms is this?
questions.explanation: Intellectualization is a defence mechanism whereby a person deals with and avoids emotional difficulties using excessive abstract thinking. The person excessively uses intellectual processes to avoid affective expression or experience. Undue emphasis is focused on the inanimate to avoid intimacy with people, attention is paid to external reality to avoid the expression of inner feelings and stress is excessively placed on irrelevant details to avoid perceiving the whole.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not a characteristic of Milieu Group Therapy?
questions.explanation: Rapaport described the four characteristics in Milieu Group Therapy: democratization (equal sharing of power); permissiveness (tolerance of others’ behaviour); reality confrontation (confronting the views of others); and communalism (sharing of amenities). Most milieu therapy programmes, such as therapeutic communities, emphasize group and social interaction; rules and expectations are mediated by peer pressure for normalization of adaption. When patients are viewed as responsible human beings, adoption of the passive patient role becomes reduced.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most important factor for effective psychotherapy?
questions.explanation: Therapeutic alliance is the single best predictor of benefit for psychotherapy. It is key for the therapist to develop trust and respect between the therapist and the client. It is also essential for the therapist to demonstrate empathy.

questions.question_text: Childhood-onset bipolar disorder has been known to be rare. Which of the following psychiatric comorbidities is it commonly associated with?
questions.explanation: Previous research has found an association with that of ADHD. The core clinical features include reduction of sleep. The first-line of treatment is that of olanzapine. In particular, childhood bipolar disorder has been ranked as having the second worst prognosis among all the psychiatric disorders in childhood.

questions.question_text: A 50-year-old woman has strong family history of depression, and she is being prescribed with venlafaxine 225 mg ON and mirtazapine 45 mg ON for 6 months. She is admitted for severe depressive episode, but she refuses electroconvulsive therapy (ECT) and psychotherapy. She does not have any other medical illnesses. Which of the following treatment strategies is recommended?

options.text: Augment with mianserin, continue with venlafaxine and mirtazapine
Augment with mianserin, continue with venlafaxine but stop mirtazapine
Augment with lithium, continue with venlafaxine and mirtazapine
Augment with lithium, continue with venlafaxine but stop mirtazapine
Augment with lamotrigine, continue with venlafaxine and mirtazapine

correct_answer.text: Augment with lithium, continue with venlafaxine and mirtazapine

correct_answers.text: Augment with lithium, continue with venlafaxine and mirtazapine

questions.explanation: Based on NICE guidelines, a trial of lithium augmentation should be considered for patients whose depression has failed to respond to several antidepressants such as venlafaxine and mirtazapine. Augmentation with lithium has better evidence than augmentation with mianserin. Removing the current antidepressants might worsen the patient’s existing mood state.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old woman suffers from anorexia nervosa, and she is 30 weeks’ pregnant. The neonatologist consults you on the potential complications for her foetus. Which of the following is not known to be found in foetuses born by mothers suffering from anorexia nervosa?

options.text: Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration (APGAR) score of 2 at 1 minute and 3 at 5 minutes

correct_answer.text: Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration (APGAR) score of 2 at 1 minute and 3 at 5 minutes

correct_answers.text: Appearance, Pulse, Grimace, Activity, Respiration (APGAR) score of 2 at 1 minute and 3 at 5 minutes

questions.explanation: The majority of the women with eating disorders have normal length of pregnancy (mean length = 39 weeks). Their babies usually have normal Apgar score (at 1 and 5 minutes after birth, the scores are 8 and 9 points, respectively).

questions.question_text: A core trainee has informed you that a patient taking quetiapine has developed amenorrhoea with raised prolactin. Which one of the following actions is correct?

options.text: Reassure the patient that it is due to quetiapine
No further intervention and check the prolactin level in 3 months
Order a computed tomography (CT) brain scan
Order a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain scan

correct_answer.text: Order a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain scan

correct_answers.text: Order a magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) brain scan

questions.explanation: Quetiapine has a high affinity for muscarinic receptors. It carries the lowest risk for Extra Pyramidal Side Effect (EPSE). It carries the lowest risk of sexual dysfunction. It carries low risk for hyperprolactinaemia.

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old woman was admitted to the psychiatric ward after the accidental death of her son, which occurred 3 months ago. She complains of low mood, poor sleep, poor appetite and hearing her son’s voice. What is the diagnosis?

options.text: Bereavement – phase I: shock and protest

questions.explanation: It is important to understand and comprehend the differences between depression and bereavement. The following features are more common in depression but not in bereavement, and they include active suicidal ideations, depressive symptoms that are out of proportion with loss, feelings of guilt not related to the deceased, marked functional impairment for longer than 2 months, marked psychomotor changes lasting more than a few days and preoccupation with worthlessness.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old university student attested to the consumption of cannabis out of curiosity. He has just consumed it around 4 hours again. Which of the following is not one of the symptoms he would experience?
questions.explanation: In the acute intoxication of cannabis, the clinical signs usually include conjunctival injection, dry mouth, tachycardia as well as increased appetite. Other associated behavioral changes include anxiety or agitation, auditory, visual or tactile illusions, depersonalization, euphoria and dis-inhibition and hallucinations with preserved orientation. There will be impaired judgement, attention or reaction time. There will also be suspiciousness or paranoid ideations. There is also temporal slowing, or a sense that time is passing very slowly, or rapid flow of ideas.

questions.question_text: Interpersonal psychotherapy (IPT) is a form of talking therapy for treating depression. Which of the following is not a component of this therapy?
questions.explanation: IPT focuses on four problem areas: grief, interpersonal disputes, role transitions and interpersonal deficits. It does not address deep psychodynamic conflicts.

questions.question_text: Behaviour activation in psychotherapy includes which of the following?
questions.explanation: Behavioural activation primarily involves activity scheduling—planning and engaging in activities that provide pleasure or mastery to counteract withdrawal and inactivity.

questions.question_text: A 67-year-old man with terminal lung cancer consciously puts his illness ‘out of his mind’ and tries to enjoy life to the maximum by doing voluntary work. Which of the following defence mechanisms is he using?
questions.explanation: Suppression is the conscious decision to postpone or avoid thinking about distressing thoughts; unlike repression, it is a deliberate act.

questions.question_text: Approximately what percentage of adolescent males will kill themselves within 5 years after their first episode of suicide attempt?
questions.explanation: Studies have found that about 11% of adolescent males die by suicide within five years of a first suicide attempt.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is not one of the biological factors commonly associated with children who are diagnosed with conduct disorder?
questions.explanation: Conduct disorder is associated with low serotonin, excess testosterone, low cholesterol and low skin conductance (low skin tolerance). High dopamine is not a typical finding.

questions.question_text: Which of the following EEG findings is most typical of patients with delirium?

options.text: Intermittent high and low voltage activities

questions.explanation: Delirium most commonly shows diffuse slowing of background activity on EEG.

questions.question_text: Which of the following helps to differentiate hyperactive from hypoactive delirium?

options.text: EEG shows diffuse increased activity for hyperactive delirium and diffuse slowing for hypoactive delirium.
Patients with hyperactive delirium are more responsive to neuroleptics than those with hypoactive delirium.
Patients with hyperactive delirium have higher mortality rates than those with hypoactive delirium.
Patients with hyperactive delirium have global cognitive deficits, while those with hypoactive delirium have selected cognitive deficits.

Patients with hyperactive delirium demonstrate features of restlessness, agitation and hypervigilance, while patients with hypoactive delirium present with lethargy, sedation and respond slowly to questioning.

correct_answer.text: Patients with hyperactive delirium demonstrate features of restlessness, agitation and hypervigilance, while patients with hypoactive delirium present with lethargy, sedation and respond slowly to questioning.

correct_answers.text: Patients with hyperactive delirium demonstrate features of restlessness, agitation and hypervigilance, while patients with hypoactive delirium present with lethargy, sedation and respond slowly to questioning.

questions.explanation: Hyperactive delirium is marked by restlessness, agitation and hypervigilance; hypoactive delirium presents with lethargy, drowsiness and slowed responses.

questions.question_text: Which of the following cancers is not generally associated with a significantly higher risk of depression?
questions.explanation: Brain, lung, oropharyngeal and pancreatic cancers have higher rates of comorbid depression. Skin cancers generally do not.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants would you prescribe for a medically ill patient who is depressed and suffers from insomnia and poor appetite?
questions.explanation: Mirtazapine has sedative effects and stimulates appetite, making it suitable for depressed patients with insomnia and anorexia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about epileptic psychosis is false?

options.text: Chronic interictal psychosis is more common than postictal psychosis.
Mesial temporal focus is a risk factor for interictal psychosis.
Postictal psychosis follows an increase in seizure frequency.
Psychotic symptoms are more common with left-sided seizure foci or temporal lobe lesions.
Postictal psychotic symptoms occur immediately following a seizure.

correct_answer.text: Postictal psychotic symptoms occur immediately following a seizure.

correct_answers.text: Postictal psychotic symptoms occur immediately following a seizure.

questions.explanation: Postictal psychosis typically occurs after a lucid interval of 1–7 days following a seizure, not immediately.

questions.question_text: A woman was arrested after killing her 10-month-old daughter. The infant is described to be very noisy and cried excessively. Which of the following conditions is the most common predisposing factor?
questions.explanation: Infanticide in this context most often occurs at the hands of a mother who becomes overwhelmed by an infant’s excessive crying.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old married woman with a history of anorexia nervosa of 8 years’ duration presents to an obstetrician asking for help with infertility. She wants medication to induce ovulation as she does not have menses. She keeps her BMI strictly at 12, eats mainly vegetables and jogs 2 km every day. She is determined that she will not gain weight. The obstetrician is worried by her request. He seeks a consultation from you. Which of the following recommendations is inappropriate?

options.text: To highlight to the obstetrician the ambivalence inherent in her request.
To explore the symbolic significance of bypassing the normal conception to achieve motherhood.
To take a full developmental history, paying particular attention to her psychosexual development and conflicts with her own parents.
To explore the psychodynamic issues relating to the patient and her partner.
To respect her request to become pregnant and offer the best intervention to induce ovulation.

correct_answer.text: To respect her request to become pregnant and offer the best intervention to induce ovulation.

correct_answers.text: To respect her request to become pregnant and offer the best intervention to induce ovulation.

questions.explanation: It would be inappropriate to simply accede to her request for ovulation induction without addressing her disordered eating, body image and the psychological factors maintaining her anorexia.

questions.question_text: 20-year-old university student presents for a consultation. She is very concerned that she might acquire schizophrenia, as her distant relative has been recently diagnosed with the condition. She is keen to know the average age of onset of schizophrenia. Which of the following is true?
questions.explanation: The typical age of onset for schizophrenia is in the early to mid-20s, peaking between 21 and 30 years.

questions.question_text: A patient on follow-up with the cardiologist for heart problems complains of low mood and seeing yellow rings around objects in his visual field. Which of the following medications could possibly be responsible for his symptoms?
questions.explanation: Digoxin toxicity can produce visual disturbances such as xanthopsia (yellow vision), as well as mood changes.

questions.question_text: For which of the following conditions would speech therapy be useful for symptomatic relief?
questions.explanation: Globus pharyngeus (sensation of a lump in the throat) often responds to voice and speech therapy techniques.

questions.question_text: Which of the following antidepressants has been shown to be of most benefit in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS)?
questions.explanation: Tricyclic antidepressants at low doses have analgesic and motility-modulating effects and are supported by trials in IBS.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman is 12 weeks pregnant. She is having a relapse of her depression. Which of the following antidepressants is contraindicated for her?
questions.explanation: Paroxetine has been linked to an increased risk of congenital cardiac defects and is generally avoided in pregnancy.

questions.question_text: Melancholic depression has been considered to be of biological origin. All the following are characteristic symptoms of this condition, with the exception of
questions.explanation: Options A, B/C and E are all characteristic. Option D is a duplicate of B and is not a separate feature.

questions.question_text: Which of the following options describes the most frequently reported psychiatric symptoms reported by the elderly?
questions.explanation: Anxiety and sleep disturbance (insomnia) are the most commonly reported psychiatric complaints in older adults.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding suicide in the elderly is true?

options.text: The highest rate is in black men above the age of 70 years.
The highest rate is in white men above the age of 70 years.
It is inversely correlated with age.
It is associated with cognitive impairment in the elderly.

correct_answer.text: The highest rate is in white men above the age of 70 years.

correct_answers.text: The highest rate is in white men above the age of 70 years.

questions.explanation: White men over age 70 have the highest suicide rates of any demographic group in many countries.

questions.question_text: With regard to the cognition changes involved in ageing, which of the following statements is not true?

options.text: Intelligence peaks at the age of 25 years and levels off until the age of 60–70 years before declining further.

Memory tests, such as the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) Revised inventory, show a classical pattern of intellectual decline, with verbal intelligence quotient (IQ) declining more than performance IQ.
Tasks that have been learnt over a lifetime, relying on over-learned abilities, are more resistant to age-related changes.
The ability to abstract a concept and apply it to a new situation declines with age, most prominently after the age of 70 years.
Reaction time is noted to increase with ageing.

correct_answer.text: Memory tests, such as the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) Revised inventory, show a classical pattern of intellectual decline, with verbal intelligence quotient (IQ) declining more than performance IQ.

correct_answers.text: Memory tests, such as the Wechsler Adult Intelligence Scale (WAIS) Revised inventory, show a classical pattern of intellectual decline, with verbal intelligence quotient (IQ) declining more than performance IQ.

questions.explanation: Performance IQ tends to decline more than verbal IQ in normal ageing, not the reverse.

questions.question_text: All the following are characteristic diagnostic features for patients with frontotemporal lobe dementia, with the exception of
questions.explanation: Fronto-temporal dementia features marked behavioral changes with primitive reflexes. Detailed visuospatial/constructional tasks are relatively preserved.

questions.question_text: All the following statements about the psychopathology of old-age psychotic disorder are true, with the exception of which one?

options.text: Almost all have at least one type of delusional belief.
Approximately 45% of them have first-rank symptoms.
The most common type of hallucination in the elderly is visual hallucinations.
Thought disorder and catatonic symptoms rarely develop.
Negative symptoms might be seen but tend to be very mild.

correct_answer.text: The most common type of hallucination in the elderly is visual hallucinations.

correct_answers.text: The most common type of hallucination in the elderly is visual hallucinations.

questions.explanation: In late-life psychotic disorders, auditory hallucinations are more common than visual. Visual hallucinations are less frequent.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements regarding Graves disease and psychiatric symptoms is false?

options.text: Anti-thyroid therapy is associated with improvement in depressive symptoms.
Common symptoms reported by patients with Graves disease include tremors, irritability and anxiety.
Graves disease is associated with hypomania.
Hyperthyroidism with anxious dysphoria is more common in older patients.
The severity of psychiatric symptoms correlates poorly with thyroid hormone levels in patients with Graves disease.

correct_answer.text: Hyperthyroidism with anxious dysphoria is more common in older patients.

correct_answers.text: Hyperthyroidism with anxious dysphoria is more common in older patients.

questions.explanation: Anxious dysphoria in hyperthyroidism is more often seen in younger patients; older patients tend to present with more apathetic features.

questions.question_text: Which of the following symptoms is not typical of a patient presenting with depression associated with Cushing syndrome?
questions.explanation: Depression in Cushing syndrome is typically associated with insomnia rather than hypersomnia.

questions.question_text: Which of the following types of cancer is least associated with depression?
questions.explanation: Lymphoma has depression rates similar to other chronic illnesses, whereas lung, oropharyngeal, pancreatic and brain cancers have markedly higher rates.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman has been diagnosed with depression and has been started on an older generation of medication known as an MAOI. She is aware that there are certain foods she needs to avoid. She was taken ill recently and consulted a physician at the emergency services. In view of her persistent abdominal pain, she was administered a dose of opioid analgesic. This increases the incidence of her having which of the following conditions?
questions.explanation: Some opioid analgesics inhibit serotonin reuptake; combined with an MAOI, this can precipitate serotonin syndrome.

questions.question_text: All the following antidepressants are safe for use in mothers who are breastfeeding with the exception of?
questions.explanation: Fluoxetine has a long half-life and higher levels in breast milk; it is best avoided in breastfeeding.

questions.question_text: Based on current research, a maintenance strategy using lithium carbonate monotherapy in bipolar disorder is likely to result in remission in approximately what percentage of individuals?
questions.explanation: Long-term lithium monotherapy achieves sustained remission in roughly half of patients with bipolar disorder.

questions.question_text: Which of the following symptoms of obsessive-compulsive disorder is most resistant to treatment?
questions.explanation: Compulsive hoarding is more refractory to both medication and behavioural therapies than other symptom dimensions.

questions.question_text: Clomipramine and SSRIs antidepressants are commonly being used to treat obsessive-compulsive disorder. What is the approximate response rate?
questions.explanation: Selective serotonergic agents including clomipramine have response rates of approximately 50% in OCD.

questions.question_text: With regard to the pharmacological management of post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD), which of the following medications would be helpful in reducing the amount of fear-induced startle?
questions.explanation: Buspirone can reduce exaggerated startle responses in PTSD by modulating serotonergic and GABAergic tone.

questions.question_text: Which of the following defence mechanisms has the highest degree of adaptivity?
questions.explanation: Humour is classified among the mature defence mechanisms and is the most adaptive.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is uncommonly associated with pica?
questions.explanation: Pica is associated with intellectual disability, pregnancy, anaemia and can lead to complications such as lead poisoning.

questions.question_text: A 20-year-old man admits to the occasional use of ‘coke’. His last use was just yesterday. How long would ‘coke’ remain in the urine sample, for the sample to be test positive?
questions.explanation: Cocaine metabolites typically remain detectable in urine for up to 72 hours after use.

questions.question_text: With regard to the genetic disorder known commonly as Digeorge syndrome, which of the following psychiatric disorders is a common comorbidity?
questions.explanation: Individuals with 22q11.2 deletion (DiGeorge) have a markedly increased risk of schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: Fragile X syndrome is known to be the most common inherited cause of learning disability. It accounts for around 10%–12% of mental retardation in men. Which of the following statements about the condition is incorrect?

options.text: It is an X-linked dominant genetic disorder with low penetrance.
The disorder is due to the presence of more than 200 tri-nucleotide CGG repeats.
The presence of tri-nucleotide repeats would lead to hyper-methylation at the fragile X mental retardation gene.
Only males are affected by this disorder.
The length of the repeats is inversely related to the intelligence quotient.

correct_answer.text: Only males are affected by this disorder.

correct_answers.text: Only males are affected by this disorder.

questions.explanation: Fragile X syndrome can affect both males and females, although males are more severely affected.

questions.question_text: What is the incidence of epilepsy in Rett syndrome?
questions.explanation: Seizures occur in over 60% of girls with Rett syndrome.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false regarding Lesch–Nyhan disease?

options.text: Hyperuricaemia is a rare feature in the variant form.
Hypoxanthine–guanine phosphoribosyl transferase activity is grossly reduced or absent.
It is associated with movement disorder.
It is an X-linked recessive disorder.
The variant form presents later and is less severe and without any self-mutilation.

correct_answer.text: Hyperuricaemia is a rare feature in the variant form.

correct_answers.text: Hyperuricaemia is a rare feature in the variant form.

questions.explanation: Hyperuricaemia is a hallmark of both classic and variant forms and is not rare in the variant.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is the most frequent cutaneous manifestation of tuberous sclerosis?
questions.explanation: Adenoma sebaceum (facial angiofibromas) are the most frequent skin lesions in tuberous sclerosis.

questions.question_text: A 10-year-old girl is noted to be always happy and smiling. She has jerking movement and ataxic gait. She has a history of epilepsy, and she studies in a special school. Which chromosome would be affected in her presentation?
questions.explanation: Angelman syndrome, characterized by a ‘happy puppet’ appearance, is caused by a maternal deletion on chromosome 15.

questions.question_text: Children who are depressed tend to present more with which of the following symptoms, compared with adults?
questions.explanation: Depressed children often show somatic complaints (headache, stomachache) rather than overt sadness.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements is false about the findings from multimodal treatment study (MTA) on ADHD?

options.text: There is a small but detectible reduction in overall growth in height for children who remain on stimulants.
Loss of growth is maximal in the first year of treatment.
35% showed a moderate and gradual improvement, and 50% showed significant improvement over the 3-year study period.
15% initially responded well but deteriorated over 3 years.
Drug treatment reduces the rate of delinquency and substance abuse in children with ADHD to the rate found in normal controls.

correct_answer.text: Drug treatment reduces the rate of delinquency and substance abuse in children with ADHD to the rate found in normal controls.

correct_answers.text: Drug treatment reduces the rate of delinquency and substance abuse in children with ADHD to the rate found in normal controls.

questions.explanation: Although stimulant treatment reduces some behavioural problems, delinquency and substance misuse remain elevated compared with controls.

questions.question_text: For adolescent-onset bipolar disorder, what percentage of adolescents has first-rank symptoms?
questions.explanation: About 20% of adolescents with bipolar disorder can exhibit Schneiderian first-rank psychotic symptoms.

questions.question_text: What is the approximate heritability of autism?
questions.explanation: Twin and family studies estimate autism heritability at around 90%.

questions.question_text: A medical student is currently on attachment to the Child and Adolescent Mental Health Services (CAMHS) unit. Of note, he has seen two children been diagnosed with chronic motor and vocal tics. With regard to the prognosis of the condition, you will advise the medical student that the disorder usually lasts for approximately how long before eventually stopping?
questions.explanation: Chronic motor and vocal tics (Tourette’s syndrome) often begin in early childhood and typically wane after about 4–6 years.

questions.question_text: Which one of the following statements regarding conduct disorder is false?

options.text: It is associated with a low plasma 5-hydroxytryptamine (5-HT) level.
It is associated with reading difficulty.
It is associated with overcrowding (>four children) environment.

questions.explanation: Conduct disorder more commonly has onset in middle childhood or early adolescence, not infancy/early childhood.

questions.question_text: With regard to the pharmacological treatment of PTSD, which of the following medications would be helpful in reducing the hyper-arousal and intrusive symptoms?
questions.explanation: Propranolol, by blocking noradrenergic hyperactivity, can reduce hyper-arousal and exacerbate intrusive symptoms in PTSD.

questions.question_text: Which of the following statements about the aetiological factors pertaining to PTSD is false?

options.text: The exaggerated physiological responses are mediated by both the noradrenergic and dopaminergic neurotransmitter systems.
There is an increase in the glucocorticoid receptors in the hippocampus.
There is a corresponding reduction in the peripheral cortisol.
There is a possible catecholaminergic mediation of PTSD symptoms.
Opioid functions have been proposed to be disturbed in PTSD.

correct_answer.text: There is an increase in the glucocorticoid receptors in the hippocampus.

correct_answers.text: There is an increase in the glucocorticoid receptors in the hippocampus.

questions.explanation: PTSD is associated with fewer hippocampal glucocorticoid receptors and lower cortisol levels, not an increase.

questions.question_text: An 8-year-old boy has frequent loss of temper, arguments with parents and feels irritable at home but not at school. These symptoms have persisted for 8 months. Which of the following treatments would you recommend?
questions.explanation: Parent management training is the first-line psychosocial intervention for oppositional defiant disorder in children.

questions.question_text: Which of the following is a 3-year-old child able to do if he or she has normal motor developmental milestones?

options.text: Build a tower of 10 cubes and copy a square
Build a tower of 10 cubes and stand on one foot

correct_answer.text: Build a tower of 10 cubes and stand on one foot

correct_answers.text: Build a tower of 10 cubes and stand on one foot

questions.explanation: By age 3, a child can build a tower of 10 cubes and can stand on one foot briefly; copying a square develops around age 4–5.

questions.question_text: Individual cohort study.
questions.explanation: A cohort study provides level 2B evidence in the CEBM hierarchy.

questions.question_text: Individual randomized controlled trials.
questions.explanation: An individual RCT provides level 1B evidence in the CEBM hierarchy.

questions.question_text: Individual case–control studies.
questions.explanation: A case–control study provides level 3B evidence in the CEBM hierarchy.

questions.question_text: A study aims to determine the effects of cannabis misuse on the incidence of schizophrenia in a community.
questions.explanation: Incidence of schizophrenia following exposure to cannabis is best studied in a cohort design.

questions.question_text: A study aims to find out if alcohol dependence is a risk factor for morbid jealousy in a community.
questions.explanation: Comparing those with jealousy (cases) and without (controls) for past alcohol dependence is a case–control study.

questions.question_text: A study examines the data from 23 member states of the European Union and investigates whether television exposure is related to fear of terrorism. This study is controlled for population size, education level, age distribution and income.
questions.explanation: The unit of analysis is populations of countries, making this an ecological study.

questions.question_text: A study aims to find out if long-term aspirin use in patients with ischaemic heart disease protects against dementia.
questions.explanation: A case–control study comparing those with dementia (cases) and without (controls) on past aspirin use is appropriate.

questions.question_text: A study aims to find out the prevalence of schizophrenia in San Francisco.
questions.explanation: Measuring prevalence of schizophrenia at one point in time is a cross-sectional study.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old woman presents with irritability and increasing inability to concentrate. She is also getting more forgetful, and she finds herself having difficulty walking. She has had two seizures over the last 3 months. On further enquiry, her aunt also has similar problems.
questions.explanation: Familial subcortical dementia with seizures and gait difficulty fits CADASIL.

questions.question_text: A 54-year-old man presents with a gradual change in behaviour over the past 2 years. He was previously soft-spoken and reserved but is now very vocal and argumentative. He insists on driving despite having previously knocked into curbs because of poor judgement. He does not consider himself to be forgetful.
questions.explanation: Behavioural disinhibition with preserved memory suggests fronto-temporal dementia.

questions.question_text: A 45-year-old woman lost her husband in a fire 2 months ago. Since then, she has been complaining of persistent memory loss and forgetfulness. She is also lethargic, has no appetite and is not sleeping well. When she is asked to perform the Mini Mental State Examination, most of her answers are ‘I don’t know’.
questions.explanation: Depression with 'don’t know' responses and psychomotor slowing mimics dementia (pseudodementia).

questions.question_text: A 55-year-old man fell off a ladder and knocked his head against a wall about 2 weeks ago. Since then, he has been having memory problems, difficulty walking and difficulty passing urine.
questions.explanation: The triad of gait disturbance, dementia and urinary incontinence after trauma suggests normal pressure hydrocephalus.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old woman is brought in by the police for psychiatric assessment, as she was found wandering around the streets. She is unable to provide any personal details about herself and appears to be in a daze. Her son, with whom she is very close, died in a road traffic accident a few days ago. All physical investigations are normal.
questions.explanation: A dissociative fugue presents with wandering, amnesia and dazed appearance following trauma.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man presents with fluctuating memory loss with mood swings. He has slurred speech and left-sided muscle weakness. He has multiple medical comorbidities, including poorly controlled hypertension and diabetes.
questions.explanation: Stepwise cognitive decline with focal deficits in a hypertensive, diabetic patient indicates vascular dementia.

questions.question_text: A 75-year-old woman presents with memory loss, fluctuating consciousness and poor gait. She has very few facial expressions and appears to be stiff on walking. She has had several falls over the course of 6 months. She also mentions that she sees little children running across the ward in the middle of the night.
questions.explanation: Parkinsonism with visual hallucinations and fluctuations suggests Lewy body dementia.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old man is brought in by the police to the hospital for assessment, as he was found wandering the streets. When the doctor speaks to him, he says that he is here to meet a friend who was hospitalized and that he has seen the doctor before. Medical records show that he has been a chronic heavy alcohol drinker.
questions.explanation: Confabulation, amnesia and chronic heavy drinking indicate Korsakoff psychosis.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman with a diagnosis of anorexia nervosa is brought in to the hospital after she fainted while running on the treadmill for 2 hours. Her BMI is 15. According to her family, she has been refusing food and taking medication to induce vomiting. She is given intravenous dextrose solution for fluid replacement in the emergency department. She subsequently becomes confused, and neurological examination reveals horizontal diplopia and ataxia. Her family says that she does habitually drink alcohol.
questions.explanation: Glucose infusion without thiamine in a malnourished patient precipitates Wernicke encephalopathy.

questions.question_text: Anorexia nervosa. (Male:female ratio)
questions.explanation: Anorexia nervosa occurs about ten times more often in females than males.

questions.question_text: Bulimia nervosa. (Male:female ratio)
questions.explanation: Bulimia nervosa also shows a roughly 1:10 male-to-female ratio.

questions.question_text: Post-traumatic stress disorder. (Male:female ratio)
questions.explanation: PTSD is about twice as common in females as in males.

questions.question_text: Social phobia. (Male:female ratio)
questions.explanation: Social phobia occurs equally in males and females.

questions.question_text: Suicide. (Male:female ratio)
questions.explanation: Completed suicide rates are about three times higher in males than females.

questions.question_text: Depressive disorder. (Male:female ratio)
questions.explanation: Depressive disorders are about twice as common in females as in males.

questions.question_text: Schizophrenia. (Male:female ratio)
questions.explanation: Schizophrenia has an approximately equal gender distribution.

questions.question_text: Short stature.
questions.explanation: Prader–Willi syndrome is characterized by short stature and obesity.

questions.question_text: Tall stature.
questions.explanation: Homocystinuria (Marfanoid habitus) presents with tall stature.

questions.question_text: Microcephaly.
questions.explanation: Cri du chat syndrome features microcephaly and characteristic cat-like cry.

questions.question_text: Macrocephaly.
questions.explanation: Neurofibromatosis often presents with macrocephaly and cutaneous neurofibromas.

questions.question_text: Hyperactivity and aggression.
questions.explanation: Phenylketonuria, if untreated, leads to hyperactivity, aggression and intellectual disability.

questions.question_text: Which antipsychotic is not recommended for patients with liver impairment?
questions.explanation: Chlorpromazine undergoes extensive hepatic metabolism and carries high risk in liver impairment.

questions.question_text: Which antidepressants could be used for patients with liver impairment? (choose two)
questions.explanation: Paroxetine and citalopram have safer hepatic profiles compared with tricyclics and fluoxetine.

questions.question_text: Which mood stabilizers are indicated for patients with liver impairment?
questions.explanation: Lithium is excreted renally and does not require hepatic metabolism.

questions.question_text: Which mood stabilizers are not indicated for patients with liver impairment? (choose two)
questions.explanation: Carbamazepine and valproate are hepatically metabolized and pose risks in liver impairment.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of this psychiatric condition in patients with HIV is around 1.5%. If it presents early in the course of the infection, it is usually associated with social problems. If it presents late in the course of the HIV infection, it is usually associated with HIV dementia. Which psychiatric condition is this?
questions.explanation: Manic episodes occur in about 1.5% of HIV patients and may relate to social stress early and dementia later.

questions.question_text: This is a common psychiatric condition that usually occurs immediately after the diagnosis of HIV infection. The patient may present in a state of shock, with depersonalization and de-realization.
questions.explanation: An acute stress reaction is common immediately after receiving an HIV diagnosis.

questions.question_text: The prevalence of this psychiatric condition in people with HIV is around 30%. It is more frequent in the period following the identification of the seropositive HIV infection or even in the initial stages of HIV dementia.
questions.explanation: Depression affects about 30% of HIV-positive individuals, especially early in the disease.

questions.question_text: This usually occurs late into the course of the illness, especially when there is significant immunosuppression.
questions.explanation: HIV-associated dementia occurs late in the course with profound immunosuppression.

questions.question_text: Mild mental retardation accounts for approximately what percentage of all learning disabilities?
questions.explanation: Mild intellectual disability constitutes about 80% of all cases.

questions.question_text: Moderate mental retardation accounts for approximately what percentage of all learning disabilities?
questions.explanation: About 10% of intellectual disability cases are classified as moderate.

questions.question_text: Severe mental retardation accounts for approximately what percentage of all learning disabilities?
questions.explanation: Severe intellectual disability makes up roughly 3% of cases.

questions.question_text: Profound mental retardation accounts for approximately what percentage of all learning disabilities?
questions.explanation: Profound intellectual disability is about 2% of all cases.

questions.question_text: Which is a characteristic feature of Klinefelter syndrome?

options.text: Wide sandal gap between first and second toes

questions.explanation: Testicular atrophy and infertility are key features of Klinefelter syndrome (XXY).

questions.question_text: Which are characteristic features of fragile X syndrome?

options.text: Wide sandal gap between first and second toes

questions.explanation: Fragile X features macrocephaly, gaze aversion and a high-arched palate among other signs.

questions.question_text: Which are characteristic features of Down syndrome?

options.text: Wide sandal gap between first and second toes

correct_answers.text: Wide sandal gap between first and second toes

questions.explanation: Down syndrome commonly presents with conductive hearing loss, almond eyes, epicanthic folds and sandal gap.

questions.question_text: Which are characteristic features of Turner syndrome?

options.text: Wide sandal gap between first and second toes

questions.explanation: Turner syndrome is marked by a shield chest, widely spaced nipples, ovarian dysgenesis and often a high-arched palate.

questions.question_text: This model allows for within-study variability only.
questions.explanation: Fixed-effect models account for within-study variability but assume a common effect size.

questions.question_text: This model allows for within- and between-study variation and adds in the effects of moderators.
questions.explanation: Mixed-effects models incorporate both within- and between-study variability and moderator effects.

questions.question_text: This model does not allow specification of within-study variation.
questions.explanation: Simple meta-regression does not model within-study variance explicitly.

questions.question_text: A 35-year-old man has a long-standing history of chronic cough as well as associated dyspnoea. He has not been a smoker all his life and has not been exposed to passive smoking. Recently, he decided to seek a consult, as he finds that he has been having difficulties with his memories. In addition, he has been having some fixed and unshakable beliefs.
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis can cause pulmonary symptoms and neuropsychiatric manifestations including memory impairment and delusions.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old university student is here for a consultation with the General Psychiatry service. She reports feeling increasingly low in her mood with associated symptoms of marked lethargy. She shared that a few months ago, her friends and family commented that she has had a malar rash on her face.
questions.explanation: Systemic lupus erythematosus often presents with malar rash and neuropsychiatric symptoms.

questions.question_text: A 25-year-old woman has been having symptoms of hypersomnolence despite having a good night’s rest. Her general practitioner has run some routine labs, and it was noted that she has elevated calcium levels.
questions.explanation: Sarcoidosis can cause hypercalcemia leading to fatigue and hypersomnolence.

questions.question_text: A 65-year-old man has been referred to the psycho-geriatrics service for worsening visual hallucinations. On clinical examination, the core trainee noted that the patient has rather severe tremors, which are predominantly on the right side. In addition, reduced arm swing and a typical gait (small steps and shuffling gait) were noted.
questions.explanation: Parkinson’s disease presents with unilateral tremor, shuffling gait and visual hallucinations in advanced stages.

questions.question_text: A 38-year-old man has been referred to the psychiatrist for an evaluation by his neurologist. Of note, his family has noted that he would cry uncontrollably at times without any reasons. Of late, he has been requiring more assistance in his activities of daily living from his family members.
questions.explanation: Pseudobulbar affect with progressive motor decline and need for assistance suggests ALS.

questions.question_text: A 60-year-old woman has been referred as she has been having much memory impairment of late. In addition, she has been having frequent falls as well.
questions.explanation: PSP features early falls, vertical gaze palsy and cognitive decline.

questions.question_text: A 26-year-old man has been referred to the psychiatrist for an assessment. Of late, his wife has noted that he has a marked change in terms of his personality. At times, he has been noted to be irritable and impulsive. In addition, he has been noted to be increasingly clumsy.
questions.explanation: Early personality changes, irritability, impulsivity and motor incoordination fit Huntington’s disease.

questions.question_text: What is the increase in risk of acquiring schizophrenia if a person is of the male gender?
questions.explanation: Schizophrenia has an approximately equal incidence in males and females, so there is no increased risk based on gender.

questions.question_text: What is the increase in risk of acquiring schizophrenia if an individual is of Afro-Caribbean ethnicity in the United Kingdom?
questions.explanation: Studies in the UK show that Afro-Caribbean individuals have about a twofold increased risk of schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: What is the increase in risk of an individual acquiring schizophrenia if he has been using cannabis on a long-term basis?
questions.explanation: Long-term cannabis use approximately doubles the risk of developing schizophrenia.

questions.question_text: What is the increase in risk of an individual acquiring psychosis if he has been using cannabis on a long-term basis?
questions.explanation: Long-term cannabis use increases the risk of psychotic experiences about fourfold.

questions.question_text: The staff of a hostel for learning disability patients want to train their clients to clean up the tables after meals. They develop a successive reinforcing schedule to reward their clients. The clients will be rewarded successively over time for removing their utensils from the dining table into the kitchen. Then they need to wash and dry the utensils and put them back into the right drawers. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: This	phenomenon	is	known	as	shaping

questions.question_text: A 2-year-old son of a woman is scared of dogs. His mother tries to reduce his fear by bringing him to see the dogs in the park. The fear-provoking situation is coupled and opposed by putting him on her lap and allowing him to drink his favourite juice. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Reciprocal inhibition is based on counterconditioning — pairing a fear-evoking stimulus with a positive, relaxing response to reduce fear.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old woman staying in London develops fear of the tube (underground metro), and she sees a psychologist for psychotherapy. The psychologist has drafted a behavioural programme in which the patient is advised to start with travelling between two tube stations with her husband and gradually increase this to more stations without her husband. At the end of the hierarchy, she will travel alone on the long journey from a Heathrow terminal station to Cockfosters station along almost the entire length of the Piccadilly line. (Choose one option.)
questions.explanation: Systematic desensitization involves creating a graded hierarchy of feared situations and gradually exposing the patient while teaching relaxation techniques to reduce anxiety.

questions.question_text: The neonate developed floppy baby syndrome after he was born. On physical examination, it was noted to have cleft palate.
questions.explanation: In utero benzodiazepine exposure near term can cause floppy infant syndrome and features like cleft palate.

questions.question_text: The 4-year-old child developed attention deficit and hyperactivity.
questions.explanation: Maternal tobacco use is associated with increased risk of attention-deficit/hyperactivity in children.

questions.question_text: The infant was noted to be irritable. On physical examination, he has a small head with short eye openings. The cardiovascular examination reveals a heart murmur. The health visitor measures his length regularly, and it is obvious that the infant has growth retardation.
questions.explanation: Fetal alcohol syndrome causes IUGR, microcephaly, facial dysmorphism and congenital heart defects.

questions.question_text: The infant develops fever, inability to sleep, and poor feeding 3 days after birth. Due to repeating vomiting and diarrhoea, he appears to be dehydrated with poor weight gain since birth. On physical examination, he appears to be irritable and exhibits yawning and sneezing. The tone in upper limbs and lower limbs is increased.
questions.explanation: Neonatal abstinence syndrome from maternal opiate use presents with fever, feeding difficulties, irritability, autonomic signs and hypertonia.

questions.question_text: A 68-year-old woman with history of diabetes was referred by the geriatrician for assessment for depression. She complains of low mood and weight loss. Physical examination reveals oedema in her lower limbs. Echocardiogram shows congestive heart failure. Her medications include fluoxetine, metformin and furosemide.
questions.explanation: Furosemide can cause diuretic-induced weight loss and may contribute to low mood via electrolyte disturbances. Fluoxetine	is	stronger	than	other	SSRIs	in	causing	anorectic	effect.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old Irish woman was referred by her GP for assessment of depression. She complains of having lethargy, frequent diarrhoea with offensive stool and weight loss. She appears to be pale, and physical examination shows clubbing, abdominal distension and oral ulceration. Barium follow-through is abnormal. Her medications include iron and vitamin D supplements.
questions.explanation: Malabsorption with diarrhea, weight loss, pale appearance, clubbing and abnormal barium study suggest coeliac disease.

questions.question_text: A 16-year-old girl was referred by the paediatrician for assessment of depression. She was admitted due to fever, weight loss, diarrhoea and abdominal pain. She appears to be thin and pale. Physical examination shows clubbing, aphthous ulceration, abdominal tenderness and perianal skin tags. She is a smoker. Her medication includes paracetamol, and she is currently nil by mouth.
questions.explanation: Crohn’s disease causes fever, weight loss, diarrhea, abdominal pain, clubbing, aphthous ulcers and perianal disease.

questions.question_text: A 40-year-old man was referred by the rheumatologist for assessment of depression. He complains of weight loss and migratory polyarthritis and appears to be pale. Physical examination reveals clubbing and pigmentation. His medications include sulphamethoxazole and trimethoprin.
questions.explanation: Whipple’s disease presents with migratory arthritis, weight loss, malabsorption signs and hyperpigmentation.

questions.question_text: A 30-year-old woman was referred by her GP for the management of depression and anxiety. She complains of loose stool, palpitations and tremor. Her hair appears to be very wet, as if she has just washed her hair without drying. Her medication includes alprazolam 0.25 mg TDS.
questions.explanation: Hyperthyroidism causes anxiety, diarrhea, palpitations, tremor and hyperhidrosis ('wet hair').

questions.question_text: A 16-year-old male adolescent was referred to you by the paediatrician after a suicide attempt. He had recently broken up with his girlfriend. He was criticized of being too fat. He has rapid weight loss, and he is still very dissatisfied with his body shape. He is very preoccupied with the amount of calories consumed and tries to avoid all carbohydrate- or lipid-rich foods.
questions.explanation: This presentation—rapid weight loss, body image disturbance, calorie restriction—fits anorexia nervosa.
